lesson.title: Reflexives & Daily Life
lesson.subtitle: me llamo, levantarse, acostarse — reflexives as self-action and daily routine

hook.title: You Have Spoken Reflexive Spanish Since Day One!
hook.content: Remember Me llamo Alex ('I call myself Alex') from your very first greeting branch? That is a reflexive verb! Whenever the dictionary form of a verb has **-se** hooked onto the end — like llamarse ('to call oneself'), levantarse ('to lift oneself / get up'), or acostarse ('to lay oneself down / go to bed') — the action reflects back onto the subject using **me** ('myself'), **te** ('yourself'), **se** ('himself/herself/usted/themselves'), and **nos** ('ourselves / each other')!

pattern.title: Peeling Off '-se' and Putting It in Front
pattern.content: To conjugate levantarse ('to get up'): peel off -se, move it in front of the verb to match the person, and conjugate levantar normally: Yo **me levanto** ('I get up'), Tú **te levantas** ('You get up'), Él/Ella/Usted **se levanta**, Nosotros **nos levantamos**! And notice acostarse ('to go to bed'): it's an o→ue boot verb, so yo **me acuesto** ('I go to bed'), but nosotros **nos acostamos**!
pattern.linguist_note: Romance pronominal verbs cover true reflexives, reciprocals (nos vemos), and middle-voice changes of state (levantarse, dormirse).
pattern.trap_note: When a reflexive verb is an infinitive after quiero or voy a ('I want to get up' / 'I am going to get up'), remember to change -se to match the speaker: Quiero levantarme (or Me quiero levantar)!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: to go to bed (lit. lay oneself down, o→ue)
my name is (lit. I call myself)

exercises.target_answer: levantarse, me levanto, acostarse, me acuesto, me llamo, nos vemos
exercises.meaning: to get up (lit. lift oneself), I get up, to go to bed (lit. lay oneself down, o→ue), I go to bed, my name is (lit. I call myself), we see each other
exercises.explanation: Reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nos) walk in front of conjugated verbs or hook onto infinitives.

exercises.prompt: Spanish levantar ('to lift/raise', levantarse 'to get up from bed') comes from Latin levāre ('to make light / raise up'). Which English verb meaning 'to float or rise into the air' comes from the exact same root?
exercises.meaning: when you 'me levanto' in the morning, you are literally 'levitating / elevating' yourself out of bed!
exercises.explanation: Latin levāre gave Spanish levantar (plus el levante 'where the sun rises') and English levitate and elevate.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I get up at seven o'clock'?
exercises.meaning: I get up at seven o'clock
exercises.explanation: Without me, levanto means 'I lift [something else]'; to get yourself up, you need Me levanto!

exercises.meaning: I get up at eight o'clock
exercises.explanation: Me + levanto + a las ocho ('at eight o'clock').

exercises.idea: say that we will see each other tomorrow ('We see each other tomorrow')
cues: we see (1st pl. of ver) → vemos
idea_parts: We see each other → Nos vemos
exercises.meaning: See you tomorrow (lit. We see each other tomorrow)
exercises.explanation: ¡Nos vemos mañana! — in plural, nos and se also express reciprocal 'each other'!

diagnosis.cue: For 'we see each other', pair 1st-person plural nos with vemos: Nos vemos mañana.

summary.outcome: Conjugate reflexive verbs (levantarse, acostarse, llamarse) and use nos/se for reciprocal 'each other'.

use_example.german: Me levanto a las siete y nos vemos mañana.
use_example.english: I get up at seven and we'll see each other tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: Without me/te/se/nos, you lift or lay someone else; with me/te/se/nos, you get up and go to bed yourself!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2401] Morning to Night Routine): chain reflexive verbs across a full day and hook pronouns onto infinitives.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'What is your name? (How do you call yourself?)'

foreshadow.line: Next in Topic 25: the famous inverted verb gustar ('me gusta el café' = 'the coffee pleases me')!

payoff.text: The object pronouns me, te, nos from Topics 22–23 are the exact same pronouns used in reflexive verbs — only 3rd person changes to se!

levantarse.english_meaning: to get up (me levanto: I get up)
levantarse.context_translation: I get up at seven o'clock.

acostarse.english_meaning: to go to bed, lie down (me acuesto: I go to bed)
acostarse.etymology_derivation: From costa ('rib/side') = 'to lay oneself on one's side'.

llamar.context_translation: What's your name? (How do you call yourself?)
llamar.etymology_derivation: Latin clāmāre ('to call, shout') shifted initial cl- to ll-. Me llamo = 'I call myself'.

me_llamo.english_meaning: my name is (lit. I call myself)
me_llamo.etymology_derivation: Spanish introduces by reflexive verb: me llamo ('I call myself').

me.etymology_derivation: Walks left of conjugated verbs or hooks onto infinitives.

se.english_meaning: himself, herself, yourself (usted), themselves; to him/her/them (before lo/la)
se.shift_rule: Reflexive AND the 'se lo' replacement for *le lo
se.context_translation: I tell it to him/her today.
se.etymology_derivation: Whenever le or les meets lo/la/los/las, Spanish softens the tongue-twister *le lo into se lo!

nos.english_meaning: us, to us, ourselves, each other

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
